title: Given two lists of closed intervals each sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, return the list of intervals representing their intersection. Solve it with the two-pointer merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.

s1_definition.profdef: The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and produces the list of intervals where they overlap. It is solved in linear time with two pointers advancing through both lists simultaneously: at each step the overlap of the two current intervals, if any, is the maximum of their starts to the minimum of their ends, and we advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first because that interval cannot intersect anything further ahead in the other list.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has two sorted timelines, one of windows when an account was eligible for trading and one of windows when the market was open, and wants the windows when both conditions held at once. He walks both timelines together, and at each pair he takes the slice where they overlap, from the later start to the earlier end, then steps forward on whichever window closes first because it has nothing more to offer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Overlap is max-start to min-end; advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and produces the list of intervals where they overlap. It is solved in linear time with two pointers advancing through both lists simultaneously: at each step the overlap of the two current intervals, if any, is the maximum of their starts to the minimum of their ends, and we advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first because that interval cannot intersect anything further ahead in the other list.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has two sorted timelines, one of windows when an account was eligible for trading and one of windows when the market was open, and wants the windows when both conditions held at once. He walks both timelines together, and at each pair he takes the slice where they overlap, from the later start to the earlier end, then steps forward on whichever window closes first because it has nothing more to offer.

**One line to remember:** Overlap is max-start to min-end; advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first.

sections.s2_technical:
Because both lists are already sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, we can scan them together with two pointers, one into each list, without any sorting. At each step we look at the current interval from the first list and the current interval from the second list and compute their potential overlap. The overlap starts at the later of the two starts and ends at the earlier of the two ends, so `lo = Math.max(a.start, b.start)` and `hi = Math.min(a.end, b.end)`.

If that computed low is less than or equal to that computed high, the two intervals genuinely overlap and the interval from low to high is a real intersection, so we add it to the result. If low is greater than high there is no overlap at this pair, and we add nothing. Either way we must decide which pointer to advance. We advance the pointer of the interval that ends earlier, because that interval has been fully accounted for: it cannot overlap any later interval in the other list, since all later intervals start even further to the right. Concretely `if (a.end < b.end) i++; else j++;`.

A subtle correctness point is handling equal ends. If the two current intervals end at the same value, advancing either pointer is acceptable, and advancing just one is sufficient because the next iteration will reconsider the pair. The senior-level nuance is understanding why we advance based on the end rather than the start: the interval that ends first is exhausted, and keeping it would only produce duplicate or spurious comparisons. This end-based advancement is the crux of the two-pointer interval merge.

We build a fresh result list and never mutate the inputs. The time complexity is linear, O(m plus n), where m and n are the two list lengths, because each pointer advances at most through its own list once, and the space complexity is O(1) beyond the output. This two-pointer technique is the standard solution for intersecting two sorted interval lists and generalizes to merging many sorted streams.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, an automated trading account can only place orders when two independent conditions hold at the same time: the account must be within an eligibility window, and the market must be within an open-session window. Both sets of windows are maintained as sorted, non-overlapping lists. The trading engine needs the exact windows during which both conditions overlap, because only those windows are safe to trade in. This is exactly the intervals intersection problem.

Problem 2 — Comparing every eligibility window against every market window is quadratic and wasteful when both lists are already sorted. The two-pointer scan finds all overlap windows in a single linear pass over both lists, which is what lets the engine compute tradeable windows quickly at session start.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `Interval` class, a `TradingWindowService` with an `intersect` method implementing the two-pointer scan, and a runnable `IntervalIntersectionDemo` main class that intersects Rajesh's eligibility windows with the market windows, logging each overlap found at fine level and the intersection list at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's eligibility windows are [1,3] and [5,8], and the market window is a single [2,6]. We start with pointer i at 0 into eligibility and pointer j at 0 into market.

Step 1: The eligibility interval is [1,3] and the market interval is [2,6]. The overlap low is the maximum of starts 1 and 2, which is 2, and the overlap high is the minimum of ends 3 and 6, which is 3. Since 2 is less than or equal to 3, they overlap, so we add [2,3] to the result. The eligibility interval ends at 3, the market interval ends at 6, and 3 is less than 6, so we advance the eligibility pointer i to 1.

Step 2: The eligibility interval is now [5,8] and the market interval is still [2,6]. The overlap low is the maximum of 5 and 2, which is 5, and the overlap high is the minimum of 8 and 6, which is 6. Since 5 is less than or equal to 6, they overlap, so we add [5,6] to the result. The eligibility interval ends at 8, the market interval ends at 6, and 8 is not less than 6, so we advance the market pointer j to 1.

Step 3: The market pointer j has reached the end of the market list, so the loop stops.

The tradeable intersection windows for Priya are [2,3] and [5,6].

```
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma (CUR3001) eligibility = [[1,3], [5,8]], market = [[2,6]]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Overlap of [1,3] and [2,6] = [2,3]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Overlap of [5,8] and [2,6] = [5,6]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Tradeable (intersection) windows = [[2,3], [5,6]]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma tradeable windows = [[2,3], [5,6]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: eligibility [[1,3],[5,8]], market [[2,6]]
    │
    ▼
  TradingWindowService.intersect()  (two pointers i, j)
    │
    ├─ a=[1,3] b=[2,6]  lo=max(1,2)=2 hi=min(3,6)=3  2≤3 add [2,3]
    │     a.end 3 < b.end 6 → i++
    ├─ a=[5,8] b=[2,6]  lo=max(5,2)=5 hi=min(8,6)=6  5≤6 add [5,6]
    │     a.end 8 ≥ b.end 6 → j++
    └─ j exhausted → stop
    │
    ▼
  Output: [[2,3],[5,6]]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — TradingWindowService (two-pointer intersect) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Two-Pointer scan: parallel traversal of two sorted lists      │
  │   WHY: O(m+n) intersection with no sorting                    │
  │ Single Responsibility: service computes intersections only    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: service intersects; Interval holds data                    │
  │ O: generalizes to N lists via a heap, same end-advance idea   │
  │ D: engine depends on the returned List<Interval>              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │     TradingWindowService     │ ──────▶│       Interval        │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │ uses   │  - start, end: int    │
  │  + intersect(List<Interval>, │        │  + getStart/getEnd    │
  │      List<Interval>)         │        └──────────────────────┘
  │      : List<Interval>        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Key invariant ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  overlap(a,b) = [max(a.start,b.start), min(a.end,b.end)] if lo<=hi
  advance pointer of interval with smaller end (it is exhausted)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → service.intersect(eligibility, market)
  3.     → while i<m && j<n: lo=max starts, hi=min ends
  4.       → if lo<=hi add [lo,hi]
  5.       → advance i or j by smaller end
  6.   → [[2,3],[5,6]]

  Contract for intersect(List<Interval>, List<Interval>):
    Pre:  both lists sorted by start, internally non-overlapping
    Post: all overlap intervals, sorted
    Note: advance by END, not start; O(m+n), no sorting needed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and asks for the list where they overlap, and I solve it in linear time with a two-pointer scan over both lists. At each step I look at the current interval from each list and compute their potential overlap as the later of the two starts to the earlier of the two ends. If that low is at most that high, the intervals genuinely overlap and I add that computed interval to the result; otherwise there is no overlap at this pair.

The decision that makes the scan work is which pointer to advance, and I advance the one whose interval ends earlier. That interval is fully exhausted because it cannot overlap any later interval in the other list, since all later intervals start even further right, so keeping it would only produce redundant comparisons. Advancing based on the end rather than the start is the crux of the technique, and when the two ends are equal advancing either one is fine because the next iteration reconsiders the pair.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the trading-window service. An automated trading account could only place orders when two independent conditions held simultaneously, an account eligibility window and a market open-session window, both maintained as sorted non-overlapping lists, and the engine needed the exact windows where both overlapped because only those were safe to trade in. The two-pointer scan computed all tradeable windows in a single linear pass over both lists, fast enough to run at session start.

The senior-level point I make is that because both inputs are already sorted I avoid any sorting entirely and get a linear pass, and that the end-based pointer advancement is the detail a shaky candidate gets wrong by advancing on the start. I also mention that this generalizes naturally: intersecting many sorted interval lists uses the same end-advance idea coordinated by a min-heap, which shows I see the pattern behind the specific problem. Explaining the max-start-to-min-end overlap, the end-advance rule, and the generalization to N lists is what tells an interviewer I own this technique rather than having memorized one case.
